top.headline: A top House Democrat opens an inquiry into who paid for Trump Jr.'s wedding
top.blurb: The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee has opened an investigation into Russian boxing official Umar Kremlev's reported funding of Donald Trump Jr.'s May wedding, days after ProPublica reported Kremlev paid roughly $170,000 for the island rental and fireworks. Kremlev, a Putin ally, has called Trump Jr. a personal friend.

top.headline: Florida quietly pushed textbook publishers to soften climate change
top.blurb: Emails uncovered by WUSF and The Hechinger Report show Florida education officials asked science textbook publishers to water down climate content: "climate change" became "changes in the environment" in one marine science text, and "polluting" vanished from descriptions of coal plants in another. The state is now updating its science standards for the first time in nearly 20 years.

top.headline: Karnataka's voter-roll purge dropped 19% of names before objections even opened
top.blurb: Karnataka's draft electoral roll under the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision fell to 4.4 crore voters from 5.5 crore before the exercise began, a 19% drop. Voters have until September 23 to file claims and objections, though even a rejected claim can be resubmitted afterward under Form 6.

top.headline: A Russian drone struck near the Ukraine-Poland border minutes after a diplomatic train passed
top.blurb: Ukraine's rail operator says a Russian drone hit a train near the Polish border shortly after a diplomatic train carrying former UK PM Boris Johnson and former Swedish PM Carl Bildt left the same station ahead of schedule. A separate train still at the station, carrying former CIA Director David Petraeus, was undamaged; no casualties were reported.

top.headline: Thousands cross into Djibouti as Houthi advance drives a new wave of Yemeni refugees
top.blurb: More than 3,400 people have landed on Djibouti's coast fleeing renewed fighting after Houthi forces seized the Red Sea port of Mocha and pushed toward the strait separating Yemen from the Horn of Africa. The UN says the latest offensive has displaced 125,000 people since the start of the month, with fighting now shifting toward Marib, the government's last northern stronghold.

top.headline: Samson and Abhishek power India to a series-clinching win over Afghanistan
top.blurb: Sanju Samson's 57 and Abhishek Sharma's 39 chased down Afghanistan's 159 for 8 with 31 balls to spare in Delhi, and Nitish Kumar Reddy's 3 for 24 undid the Afghan innings to earn him Player of the Match. The seven-wicket win puts India 2-0 up with one T20I left in the series.

top.headline: Carlo Rovelli's new book argues there is no final, objective description of reality
top.blurb: NPR's review of physicist Carlo Rovelli's "On the Equality of All Things" finds a physicist explicitly rejecting the field's old dream of one perfectly knowable universe. Rovelli leans on relational quantum mechanics and philosophers outside the Western canon, including Nagarjuna and Zhuangzi, calling the result 'a compelling, exciting and important read.'

bengal.headline: Modi to perform Durga's Chokkhu Daan at Eden Gardens in a bid for a Guinness record
bengal.blurb: Prime Minister Modi and Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari are expected to open Bengal's Durga Puja season at Eden Gardens on Mahalaya, with 10,000 dhakis drumming at once in a performance organisers hope lands in the Guinness World Records.

bengal.headline: Bengal clears a Rs 1,000-crore infrastructure push across all of the Sundarbans
bengal.blurb: The state government has cleared roughly 500 projects across all 19 Sundarbans blocks, from embankments to small river bridges, aimed at connectivity and erosion control, with full-scale work to begin once the Puja holidays end.

travel.headline: Lonely Planet's 23 picks for fall travel, from Menorca to the Salkantay Trek
travel.blurb: Lonely Planet's editors range from Turkey's southeast coast and Spain's Menorca for quiet beaches to Seoul's kimchi festival, Nara's deer park, and hiking routes through the Dolomites and Peru's Salkantay Trek.

travel.headline: A newly named New Guinea groundsnake honors Guns N' Roses guitarist Slash
travel.blurb: Researchers describing a reddish-brown nocturnal groundsnake from Papua New Guinea's Sandaun Province named it Lielaphis slashi, the 20th confirmed species in its genus, in honor of the musician's long advocacy for snakes and zoos.

happy.headline: A carpenter's gold nugget in 1848 set off a rush that built the modern world
happy.blurb: When carpenter James Marshall spotted a nugget of gold while building a Sierra Nevada sawmill in January 1848, he set off a chain of consequences that a new history by Nathaniel Philbrick traces from the Gold Rush through the Civil War to the rise of Silicon Valley.

tech_top.headline: Inside 'Project Lily,' OpenAI's effort to have humans read your ChatGPT chats
tech_top.pm_note: OpenAI's own privacy filter "can miss uncommon identifiers or over-redact" before a contractor ever sees a chat — a reminder that a privacy safeguard is only as strong as the filter standing in front of the humans behind it.
tech_top.blurb: 404 Media reports OpenAI runs a codenamed program, Project Lily, paying hundreds of contractors through Crossing Hurdles and Mercor to read real ChatGPT prompts and rate the model's replies on a 1-7 scale. A 'Privacy Filter' strips identifying details first, but OpenAI acknowledges it can miss them, and contractors say users have no idea a person may read what they typed.

tech_top.headline: Microsoft publishes a draft rulebook for what its AI models are and aren't allowed to do
tech_top.pm_note: Microsoft is the first hyperscaler to pair pacing rhetoric with an actual governance document — a template other AI vendors' product and policy teams should expect to be measured against.
tech_top.blurb: Microsoft AI opened a six-week public comment period on a draft Code of Conduct barring its MAI models from cyberattacks, aiding nuclear weapons, or generating deepfakes, and forbidding them from using deceptive or collusive tactics to evade human oversight. CEO Satya Nadella framed it as embracing 'deliberate pacing' on alignment, echoing Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

tech_more.headline: DOJ says companies used Binance to move $1.5 billion for sanctioned Iranian oil
tech_more.blurb: The Justice Department says several companies relayed roughly $1.5 billion for black-market Iranian oil sales to Chinese buyers through Binance; the exchange says it has since cut off two of the clients involved.

tech_101.text: OpenAI's internal name for the contractor pipeline that reviews real ChatGPT conversations to rate and improve the model's answers — a reminder that "an AI reads your chat" often means a person eventually does too.

A company's self-written rulebook for how its own AI models should behave, distinct from any government regulation. Microsoft's draft is the first from a major hyperscaler paired with a public comment period.

science.headline: Engineered yeast turns plastic bottles into 3D-printed protein cookies
science.blurb: Researchers broke down PET plastic and crop waste with a high-pressure water-and-oxygen process, then fed the pieces to engineered yeast strains that produced proteins, fats and even vanilla flavoring, extruded into protein-rich cookies. The system, developed partly for NASA's Deep Space Food Challenge, targets plastic pollution and food insecurity at once.

science.headline: Black holes blast winds 100 times more powerful than astronomers thought
science.blurb: Tohoku University researchers found that winds driven by supermassive black holes carry energy roughly 300,000 light-years beyond their host galaxies, about 100 times more than earlier estimates suggested. The finding shows black holes can reshape gas across scales far larger than the galaxies containing them.

science.headline: The tile that broke a decades-old math problem now twists light into pinwheels
science.blurb: University of Tokyo physicists shone laser light through the 'einstein tile,' the long-sought shape that covers a surface without ever repeating, and found it diffracts light into pinwheel-shaped chiral patterns nobody had predicted. The unexpected optical signature could point toward new ways of controlling light and polarization in optical devices.

philosophy.headline: Epistemology starts from a simple, uncomfortable fact: we get things wrong
philosophy.blurb: Aeon's introduction to epistemology begins with human fallibility, then branches into what thinking itself amounts to and what could justify believing one thing over another. Since true thoughts carry no special glow marking them as true, the essay argues, sorting good beliefs from bad is the field's real, unglamorous work.

philosophy.headline: Maybe 'free will or determinism' is the wrong question to be asking
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Meghan Griffith challenges the assumption baked into most free will debates — that we must be either free or determined, not both and not neither. She asks whether determinism is really the only threat to freedom, or simply the most obvious one to name.

philosophy_101.text: What's supposed to separate a credible belief from a baseless one, given that true beliefs don't announce themselves as true — the central puzzle epistemologists call the problem of justification.

The view that free will can survive a fully determined universe, because freedom was never about being uncaused in the first place — one of several answers to the free will/determinism debate, alongside hard determinism and libertarian free will.
